WASHINGTON (CNN) -- Sen. Hillary Clinton's chief presidential campaign strategist is quitting his post amid criticism of his public relations firm's contacts with the Colombian government over a pending free-trade deal, Clinton's campaign announced. Mark Penn will continue to advise Hillary Clinton's presidential campaign. Mark Penn and his political consulting firm will continue to advise the New York senator's Democratic presidential bid, but Penn will give up his job as chief strategist, campaign manager Maggie Williams said. "After the events of the last few days, Mark Penn has asked to give up his role as chief strategist of the Clinton campaign," Williams said. Clinton did not answer reporters' questions about Penn's exit during a campaign stop in New Mexico on Sunday. Penn is CEO of public relations giant Burson-Marsteller and is president of Penn, Schoen and Berland, his political consulting firm. Friday, he acknowledged he had met with the Colombian ambassador to the United States earlier in the week in his role as Burson-Marsteller's chief to discuss the pending U.S.-Colombia trade pact, which Clinton has criticized on the campaign trail. Penn called the meeting "an error in judgment that will not be repeated," and apologized. That prompted Colombia's government to fire the company Saturday, calling the remarks "a lack of respect to Colombians." Clinton and top aides were sharply critical of rival Democrat Barack Obama in February when reports indicated that his top economic adviser had suggested to a Canadian official that Obama was not as supportive of changes to the North American Free Trade Agreement as the Illinois senator claimed to be on the campaign trail. Penn said Friday that Clinton's opposition to the U.S.-Colombia pact, which the Bush administration is trying to push through Congress, "is clear and was not discussed" during his meeting with the ambassador. And Clinton spokesman Mo Elleithee said Penn's meeting was "not in any way done on behalf of the campaign." But Pennsylvania Gov. Ed Rendell -- a key Clinton backer in his state's April 22 primary -- suggested Sunday that Penn needed to go. "I think you've got to make it very clear for someone who is a consultant, who you are representing and who you are not representing, and I would hope that Mr. Penn, when he talked to the Colombians, made that clear. And it doesn't sound to me like he did, and that's something the campaign should take into question," Rendell told NBC's "Meet the Press." Sources in the Clinton campaign said that Penn realized this weekend that he needed to step aside, and that Clinton was disappointed that he had met with the Colombians. E-mail to a friend .

Mark Penn and his political consulting firm will continue to advise the New York senator’s Democratic presidential bid, but Penn will relinquish his position as chief strategist, campaign manager Maggie Williams said.

“After the events of the last few days, Mark Penn has asked to give up his role as chief strategist of the Clinton campaign,” Williams said.

Clinton did not respond to reporters’ questions about Penn’s departure during a campaign stop in New Mexico on Sunday.

Penn is the CEO of public relations giant Burson-Marsteller and president of Penn, Schoen and Berland, his political consulting firm. On Friday, he acknowledged that earlier in the week he had met with the Colombian ambassador to the United States in his capacity as head of Burson-Marsteller to discuss the pending U.S.-Colombia trade pact, which Clinton has criticized on the campaign trail.

Penn described the meeting as “an error in judgment that will not be repeated” and apologized. In response, Colombia’s government dismissed the company on Saturday, characterizing Penn’s remarks as “a lack of respect to Colombians.”

In February, Clinton and her top aides sharply criticized Democratic rival Barack Obama after reports indicated that his top economic adviser had suggested to a Canadian official that Obama was not as supportive of changes to the North American Free Trade Agreement as the Illinois senator had claimed on the campaign trail.

Penn said Friday that Clinton’s opposition to the U.S.-Colombia pact, which the Bush administration is seeking to push through Congress, “is clear and was not discussed” during his meeting with the ambassador. Clinton spokesman Mo Elleithee also said Penn’s meeting was “not in any way done on behalf of the campaign.”

But Pennsylvania Gov. Ed Rendell — a key Clinton supporter in his state’s April 22 primary — suggested Sunday that Penn needed to step aside.

“I think you’ve got to make it very clear for someone who is a consultant, who you are representing and who you are not representing, and I would hope that Mr. Penn, when he talked to the Colombians, made that clear. And it doesn’t sound to me like he did, and that’s something the campaign should take into question,” Rendell told NBC’s “Meet the Press.”

Sources within the Clinton campaign said Penn realized over the weekend that he needed to step aside and that Clinton was disappointed he had met with the Colombians.

**Penn steps down as Clinton chief strategist after Colombia trade controversy**

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — Mark Penn, Hillary Clinton’s chief campaign strategist, is stepping down from that role after drawing criticism for a meeting his public relations firm held with Colombian officials about a trade agreement opposed by the Democratic presidential candidate.

The Clinton campaign announced Sunday that Penn would no longer serve as chief strategist, though he was expected to continue providing polling and advice to the campaign.

The move came after reports that Penn, who also heads the public relations firm Burson-Marsteller, met with Colombia’s ambassador to the United States to discuss promoting a proposed U.S.-Colombia free-trade agreement. Clinton has publicly opposed the deal, arguing that Colombia must do more to address violence against labor leaders before Congress approves the agreement.

Penn apologized last week, calling the meeting an “error in judgment.” Burson-Marsteller later said its contract with the Colombian government had been ended.

“After the events of the last few days, Mark Penn has asked to give up his role as chief strategist of the Clinton campaign,” campaign manager Maggie Williams said in a statement. She said Penn would continue to advise the campaign as a pollster.

The controversy erupted at a sensitive moment in the Democratic race, with Clinton and Sen. Barack Obama battling for delegates and support from working-class voters in key states. Trade has been a central issue in the campaign, particularly in industrial states where many voters blame free-trade agreements for job losses.

Obama’s campaign seized on the episode, saying it raised questions about Clinton’s commitment to opposing the Colombia trade pact.

Clinton aides sought to contain the damage, emphasizing that Penn’s meeting was not connected to the campaign and that Clinton’s position on the trade deal had not changed.

Penn has long been one of Clinton’s most influential advisers and helped shape the campaign’s message throughout the primary race. But he had also become a source of tension within the campaign, where some Democrats criticized his strategy and his firm’s corporate clients.

The shake-up marks another adjustment for Clinton’s campaign as it looks to regain momentum in the increasingly competitive Democratic nomination fight.

But inside and outside the campaign, he has also been a divisive figure, blamed by some Democrats for strategic missteps, including the campaign’s early assumption that Clinton could effectively lock up the nomination on Super Tuesday.

Rendell praised Penn’s skills as a pollster but said the campaign would benefit from clearer lines of authority and fewer controversies. He also noted that Clinton’s position on the Colombia trade agreement was clear and should not be clouded by Penn’s outside business work.

Penn’s reduced role marks one of the most visible shake-ups in Clinton’s campaign since the departure of campaign manager Patti Solis Doyle earlier in the year.
